Cardiology and hematology · published research

Platelet coagulation prevention

Some red or near-infrared protocols reduced platelet aggregation or reactivity, while a green-light experiment increased aggregation under selected conditions. A pig bypass model reported less platelet destruction. No patient trial has shown fewer clots or bleeding events.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

Platelet responses to light vary by wavelength, dose, and experimental context. Red or near-infrared exposure reduced aggregation, reactivity, or platelet loss in some laboratory and animal models, while other conditions increased aggregation or activation.

Summary of the Evidence

Laboratory and animal findings are mixed rather than uniformly anti-clotting. Some visible-red and near-infrared protocols reduced platelet aggregation or reactivity, while selected green, red, or polychromatic exposures increased aggregation, degranulation, or activation. These mechanistic outcomes do not show that PBM prevents thrombosis or bleeding in patients.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical trial has treated patients with PBM to prevent thrombosis or bleeding. One publication paired mouse experiments with observational human data about lens filtering, but it did not expose patients to PBM or test clinical outcomes (Andraska et al. 2025). An ex-vivo human-blood study found that far-red light combined with nitrite decreased several coagulation measures, while light alone produced mixed results. This does not establish treatment efficacy in people (Wajih et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

In mice, visible red-light exposure was associated with reduced platelet aggregation, venous-thrombus weight, and stroke infarct size (Andraska et al. 2025). A related pig cardiopulmonary-bypass model reported less platelet loss and more stable platelet markers during extracorporeal circulation (Drohomirecka et al. 2018). Neither model establishes prevention of thrombosis or bleeding in patients.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Near-infrared exposure of porcine blood reversibly reduced platelet reactivity and modestly reduced hemolysis in a dose-dependent laboratory experiment (Walski et al. 2022). Other experiments reported anti-aggregatory effects with red light, while green light increased aggregation in the presence of weak agonists and higher-power red exposure caused degranulation. Platelet-storage studies reported better preservation of selected quality markers after 830-nm exposure, but did not test patient outcomes (Zhang et al. 2019).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Experiments span blue and green visible light, red and far-red visible light around 617–662 nm, and near-infrared exposure around 700–1000 nm. Blood was usually irradiated outside the body; other work used animal exposure or platelet-storage bags. Doses and biological contexts differ substantially, and no patient dose-finding study was identified.

Interpretation

Platelet responses are wavelength-, dose-, and context-dependent, with both inhibitory and activating findings. The evidence is mechanistic and preclinical. No clinical study shows that PBM prevents thrombosis or improves bleeding outcomes.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for preventing thrombosis or bleeding outcomes in patients.

Very low mechanistic evidence for platelet changes under specific exposures.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Laboratory and animal studies report both inhibitory and activating platelet effects, depending on wavelength, dose, co-treatment, and model. The observational human data did not test a PBM intervention, and no patient trial has shown fewer clots or bleeding events. Standardized independent studies and controlled clinical outcomes would be needed for stronger certainty.
